title: Why Indonesia has a wet season and a dry season
text:
In many parts of the world, the year is divided into four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. In most of Indonesia, however, people talk about only two: the wet season and the dry season. Both are caused by the monsoon, a wind that changes direction at different times of the year.

To understand the monsoon, it helps to know that land and sea heat up at different speeds. Land warms up quickly in strong sunshine and cools down quickly when the sunshine is weaker. The sea warms up and cools down much more slowly. When the air above warm land is heated, it rises, and cooler air flows in to take its place. This moving air is wind.

Indonesia lies between two huge areas of land: Asia to the north and Australia to the south. From around December to February, it is winter in Asia and summer in Australia. The air over hot Australia rises, so wind blows across the equator from cooler Asia towards Australia. On its long journey over warm seas, this wind picks up a great deal of water vapour. When the moist air reaches the islands of Indonesia, it rises, cools and condenses into thick clouds. As a result, heavy rain falls, especially in places such as Java. Because this wind arrives mostly from the west, it is known as the west monsoon.

From around June to August, the pattern is reversed. Now it is winter in Australia and summer in Asia, so the wind blows from Australia towards Asia, mostly from the east and south-east. Because it has crossed the dry land of Australia and only short stretches of sea, it carries much less moisture. Consequently, many parts of Indonesia have weeks with little or no rain. This is the dry season, brought by the east monsoon.

The changing monsoon affects daily life. Farmers plant rice so that their fields receive plenty of water in the wet season. In the dry season, some rivers become shallow and families may need to save water. Knowing when the seasons are likely to change helps people to plan ahead.

Not every part of Indonesia follows exactly the same pattern, and some years are wetter or drier than others. Even so, for millions of people, the monsoon is the clock that sets the rhythm of the year.
